questions.question: What are SSR, CSR, SSG, and ISR, and why do they exist? They are the rendering strategies that decide where and when HTML is generated — trading off performance, SEO, and freshness.
questions.title: Frontend Rendering Strategies Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: SSR (Server-Side Rendering), CSR (Client-Side Rendering), SSG (Static Site Generation), and ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) are the four rendering strategies that decide where and when a page's HTML is generated — on the server at request time, in the browser, at build time, or at build time with periodic re-generation. They exist because no single strategy is best for all pages: CSR is interactive but slow to first content and poor for SEO; SSR is SEO-friendly and fast to first paint but adds server load; SSG is fastest and cacheable but can't be personalized; ISR blends SSG's speed with freshness. Choosing the strategy per page — a marketing page as SSG, a logged-in dashboard as CSR, a news feed as ISR — is a core frontend engineering decision.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand each strategy's where-and-when of HTML generation and the trade-off (SEO, first paint, server load, freshness, personalization) — not just the acronyms.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing the acronyms without naming the trade-off each makes (CSR's SEO/first-paint cost, SSR's server cost, SSG's staleness, ISR's complexity).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame each by where+when HTML is generated (server/request, browser, build, build+revalidate), and name the trade-off: SEO, first paint, server load, freshness, personalization — choose per page.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: SSR (Server-Side Rendering), CSR (Client-Side Rendering), SSG (Static Site Generation), and ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) are the four rendering strategies that decide where and when a page's HTML is generated. SSR renders on the server per request; CSR renders in the browser after sending a near-empty shell; SSG renders at build time to static files; ISR renders at build time and re-renders on a timer. They exist because no single strategy is best for all pages: CSR is interactive but slow to first content and poor for SEO; SSR is SEO-friendly and fast to first paint but adds server load; SSG is fastest and cacheable but can't be personalized; ISR blends SSG's speed with freshness. Choosing the strategy per page — marketing as SSG, a dashboard as CSR, a news feed as ISR — is a core frontend engineering decision.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) CSR — the browser downloads a near-empty HTML + a JS bundle, which renders the page; fast after load, interactive, but slow first contentful paint and poor SEO (the crawler sees an empty shell); (2) SSR — the server renders HTML per request; fast first paint, SEO-friendly (crawler sees full HTML), but server load and harder interactivity (hydration); (3) SSG — HTML is generated once at build time and served as static files; fastest, fully cacheable (CDN), best SEO, but can't be personalized or show fresh data without a rebuild; (4) ISR — SSG with a revalidate interval; static speed with periodic freshness (regenerate on a timer or on-demand); (5) hydration — after SSR, the browser 'hydrates' the static HTML with JS to make it interactive; (6) streaming SSR / React Server Components — the modern evolution, streaming HTML as it renders.

sections.title: Per-page strategy choice for a content + app site
sections.content:
# A single site can use DIFFERENT strategies per page — and should.
#
#   Marketing homepage      -> SSG  (static, cacheable, fastest, best SEO)
#   Product listing          -> ISR  (static speed + periodic refresh of stock)
#   Logged-in dashboard      -> CSR  (personalized, highly interactive)
#   Search results           -> SSR  (SEO + fresh dynamic results per request)
#
# The trade-off each makes:
#   SSG : fastest + cacheable, but STALE (needs rebuild to update) and not
#        personalizable (the same HTML serves everyone).
#   ISR : SSG speed + freshness (revalidate every N seconds or on-demand),
#        but slightly stale within the window and more complex to reason about.
#   CSR : best interactivity, but SLOW first contentful paint and poor SEO
#        (the crawler sees an empty shell until JS runs).
#   SSR  : fast first paint + SEO (crawler sees full HTML), but server load
#        on every request and hydration cost to make it interactive.
#
#   Hydration: SSR/SSG HTML is static until the JS bundle runs and 'hydrates'
#   it -> interactive. The cost is the JS download + hydration work.

sections.title: Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is performance versus freshness and personalization: SSG/ISR are fastest but can't easily personalize; CSR personalizes but is slow to first paint and poor for SEO; SSR gives first paint and SEO but at server cost. The resolution is per-page choice — and modern frameworks (Next.js) make per-page strategy a route-level config. A second tension: SSR's hydration is expensive (ship HTML, then ship JS to make it interactive) — React Server Components and streaming SSR are the ecosystem's answer to ship less JS and hydrate less. The third: ISR's freshness window means data can be stale up to the revalidate interval — acceptable for a product listing, not for a live score.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: SSR/CSR/SSG/ISR decide where+when HTML is generated (server/request, browser, build, build+revalidate) — choose per page.
CSR is interactive but slow to first paint and poor for SEO; SSR is SEO-friendly but adds server load and hydration cost.
SSG is fastest and fully cacheable (CDN) but stale and not personalizable; ISR blends SSG speed with periodic freshness.
Hydration is the cost of SSR/SSG: ship HTML, then ship JS to make it interactive — React Server Components reduce this.
The right pattern is hybrid: per-page strategy (marketing=SSG, dashboard=CSR, feed=ISR, search=SSR).
ISR's freshness window means staleness up to the revalidate interval — fine for a listing, wrong for a live score.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: SSR, CSR, SSG, and ISR are the four rendering strategies that decide where and when a page's HTML is generated. SSR renders on the server per request, CSR renders in the browser after sending a near-empty shell, SSG renders at build time to static files, and ISR renders at build time and re-renders on a timer. They exist because no single strategy is best for all pages. CSR is interactive but slow to first contentful paint and poor for SEO because the crawler sees an empty shell. SSR is SEO-friendly and fast to first paint but adds server load and the cost of hydration — shipping HTML then shipping JavaScript to make it interactive. SSG is the fastest and fully cacheable on a CDN but is stale and can't be personalized without a rebuild. ISR blends SSG's speed with periodic freshness via a revalidate interval, but data can be stale up to that window, which is fine for a product listing but wrong for a live score. The right pattern is hybrid: choose the strategy per page — marketing as SSG, a logged-in dashboard as CSR, a product listing as ISR, search results as SSR. The modern evolution, React Server Components and streaming SSR, is the ecosystem's answer to the hydration cost — ship less JavaScript and hydrate less.

questions.question: Compare SSR, CSR, SSG, and ISR for a content-heavy marketing site vs a logged-in dashboard.
questions.title: Rendering Models — Marketing vs Dashboard
questions.direct_answer:
Compare SSR, CSR, SSG, and ISR for a content-heavy marketing site vs a logged-in dashboard.

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the build graph, bundler/runtime split, and deploy path), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Cache keys, personalization vs edge cache, auth cookies with CDN, RSC note.

**Classic weak answer:** ISR-stamping private user-specific HTML at the edge—cache poisoning risk.

**Senior finish:** Mention **partial prerendering** and **edge middleware** for auth gating.

interviewer_intent.testing: Cache keys, personalization vs edge cache, auth cookies with CDN, RSC note
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: ISR-stamping private user-specific HTML at the edge—cache poisoning risk
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention **partial prerendering** and **edge middleware** for auth gating

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **Rendering Models — Marketing vs Dashboard** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** Compare SSR, CSR, SSG, and ISR for a content-heavy marketing site vs a logged-in dashboard.

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Cache keys, personalization vs edge cache, auth cookies with CDN, RSC note**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **ISR-stamping private user-specific HTML at the edge—cache poisoning risk**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Mention **partial prerendering** and **edge middleware** for auth gating**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Cache keys, personalization vs edge cache, auth cookies with CDN, RSC note
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Mental model (flowchart)
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    REQ[Incoming request] --> EDGE[CDN / reverse proxy]
    EDGE -->|static assets| OBJ[(Object store / CDN)]
    EDGE -->|HTML / SSR| SSR[Node or edge SSR]
    SSR --> RSC[Render + data fetch]
    RSC --> CACHE[Set cache-control / surrogate keys]
    CACHE --> RESP[Response to browser]
    RESP --> HYDR[Client hydrate / islands]
```

| **Proof you shipped it** | Metrics (LCP, error rate), tests, DevTools trace, or incident story |

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **iSR-stamping private user-specific HTML at the edge—cache poisoning risk** and what you do instead.

sections.title: Key points (memorize this list)
sections.content:
- **Headline definition** in one sentence.
- **Mechanism:** Cache keys, personalization vs edge cache, auth cookies with CDN, RSC note
- **Pitfall:** ISR-stamping private user-specific HTML at the edge—cache poisoning risk
- **Differentiator:** Mention **partial prerendering** and **edge middleware** for auth gating
- **Proof:** DevTools / Network / Performance trace, test strategy, or metric.
- **Close:** decision rule + sensible follow-up question back to the interviewer.

sections.title: How to answer verbally (timed)
sections.content:
**Open (15–20 seconds):** Restate the question and give the one-sentence definition.

**Body (45–60 seconds):** Walk through **Cache keys, personalization vs edge cache, auth cookies with CDN, RSC note** as a story: what runs, what breaks, what you log/measure.

**Pitfall (15 seconds):** Call out **ISR-stamping private user-specific HTML at the edge—cache poisoning risk** — interviewers reward honesty about real bugs.

**Finish (15–20 seconds):** Add **Mention **partial prerendering** and **edge middleware** for auth gating**, then offer a trade-off question back (“do you optimize for TTFB or TTI here?”).

questions.question: How does Next.js App Router SSR differ from Angular Universal in operational complexity?
questions.title: Next.js App Router vs Angular Universal — Ops and Mental Model
questions.direct_answer:
How does Next.js App Router SSR differ from Angular Universal in operational complexity?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the build graph, bundler/runtime split, and deploy path), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Caching tags, incremental adoption, deployment targets, transferState.

**Classic weak answer:** Ignoring **double data fetch** without `transferState` in Angular SSR.

**Senior finish:** Mention **Resumability** / **partial hydration** trends at high level.
